hints: Notice the $8.0 \text{ N}$ weight is supported by two identical springs in parallel, so find the force carried by one spring.
Read the force against length graph for one spring: the line meets zero force at length $4.0 \text{ cm}$, so extension is length minus $4.0 \text{ cm}$.
At the force on one spring, read its length from the graph, calculate extension in $\text{m}$, then use area under the $F$-extension line $E = \frac{1}{2}Fx$.
walkthrough: The two springs are identical and in parallel, so they stretch equally and share the $8.0 \text{ N}$ load. Force on one spring is $F = 8.0/2 = 4.0 \text{ N}$.
The graph is force against length for one spring. Unstretched length is where $F=0$, which is $L_0 = 4.0 \text{ cm}$.
At $F = 4.0 \text{ N}$ the graph shows length $L = 7.0 \text{ cm}$. Extension is $x = L - L_0 = 7.0 - 4.0 = 3.0 \text{ cm} = 0.030 \text{ m}$.
Strain energy is the area under the force-extension graph: $E = \frac{1}{2}Fx$.
Substitute: $E = 0.5 \times 4.0 \text{ N} \times 0.030 \text{ m} = 0.060 \text{ J}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: With $4.0 \text{ N}$ on one spring and extension $0.030 \text{ m}$, $E = \frac{1}{2}Fx = 0.5 \times 4.0 \times 0.030 = 0.060 \text{ J}$.

B.explanation: This is twice the energy in one spring, equal to the total strain energy in both parallel springs.

C.explanation: This results from using the full spring length of about $7 \text{ cm}$ instead of the extension of $3.0 \text{ cm}$ from the $4.0 \text{ cm}$ intercept.

D.explanation: This results from giving one spring the full $8.0 \text{ N}$ load, ignoring that identical parallel springs share the load equally.
